title: Cross-border data transfer rules under the new regime
p1:
Can an Indian company store customer data on a server in the US or Singapore?

The answer may surprise you. India's new data protection framework does not automatically prohibit sending personal data overseas.
p2:
Many assume that the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act, 2023 requires all personal data of Indian citizens to remain within India.

That's not what the new framework says.

Section 16 introduces a different approach: cross-border transfers are generally permitted, but the Central Government can restrict transfers to specifically notified countries or territories.

This is commonly called a negative-list approach. Instead of approving every country individually, the Government can identify destinations where transfers are restricted.
p3:
Here's the practical insight: permission to transfer data abroad does not mean businesses are free from responsibility.

Rule 15 allows the Government to impose additional conditions concerning access to personal data by foreign governments and entities under their control.

Also, existing sector-specific restrictions, such as applicable RBI data-localisation requirements, continue to operate.

One more detail businesses should remember: Section 16 and Rule 15 are scheduled to become effective on 13 May 2027, not immediately upon notification of the 2025 Rules.

Businesses should review their cloud storage, overseas vendors and data-sharing arrangements before the new provisions take effect.
conclusion: Should Indian businesses have the freedom to transfer customer data globally, or should stricter localisation rules protect Indian users? Where would you draw the line?
